summary: NASA has run hundreds of fire experiments in microgravity and published them in its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, but the results sit in 22 separate technical tables that are hard to find, compare and interpret. EMBER is a web dashboard that cleans every NASA PSI combustion test (24 investigations, 2,029 tests) into one searchable dataset. Pick a crew environment, such as the ISS cabin, a Moon or Mars base atmosphere or a spacesuit, and EMBER shows which real NASA tests ran in similar air, which fuels and materials they cover, and where the evidence gaps are. Users can explore every test on an oxygen and pressure map, search, filter and download the data, and ask an AI assistant whose answers cite NASA sources and are checked against the evidence. Every number links back to NASA's original row, unit conversions and label fixes are disclosed, and assumed values are clearly marked. EMBER helps researchers, engineers and students see what is known about fire in space, and what is not, before the next crewed home is built.
details: What it does: EMBER turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire safety insights for crewed spacecraft, space stations, Moon and Mars bases, rovers and spacesuits. It reads every combustion investigation in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, 24 investigations in 22 data tables, and cleans them into one dataset of 2,029 tests with the same fields: fuel, fuel class, oxygen, pressure, air flow and outcome. A user picks a crew environment (ISS cabin, Shuttle EVA preparation, Exploration atmosphere, Moon Base, Mars surface habitat, spacesuit, or a custom air mix) and EMBER shows which NASA tests ran in similar oxygen and pressure, how they split across solid materials, liquid fuels, gas flames and smoke, which investigations matter most, and where the evidence gaps are, for example no solid-material tests near the richer-oxygen atmospheres planned for Moon missions. Tools include a zoomable oxygen and pressure map of every test, search, filters and CSV download, a Lab with the droplet burning law, extinction and gravity comparisons, and an AI assistant that answers in plain words, cites NASA evidence and removes any sentence whose source or number does not match. How we kept it honest: every number links back to NASA's original row, unit conversions and label corrections are disclosed, NASA values are never overwritten, and values a table leaves out are marked as assumed, cited to a source and reviewed by our team, with a researcher review still recommended. Off-topic chat questions are refused before any model call. Impact: researchers, engineers and students can see in seconds what has and has not been tested for a habitat atmosphere, which supports material selection, predictive modeling and future test planning. Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, three.js, Recharts, Node build scripts, Vercel, and Claude Haiku 5.5 with GPT-6 Luna as backup through OpenRouter. SI use: SI assistants drafted most of the code, text, visuals and the demo, and the team chose the concept, checked the science and tested the app. SI-generated visuals carry an SI mark.
